title: Wrist/Hand Active Range of Motion
purpose: Basic active range of motion (AROM) assessment of the wrist and hand: detect symptoms (pain location, quality, intensity), observe how freely the joint moves and look for compensations.
structure: Forearm (pronation/supination, at the elbow), wrist, finger MCP/PIP/DIP joints, thumb CMC/MCP/IP joints.
procedure: Patient moves actively through each direction while you observe. Standard values on the page: pronation 90 and supination 90 degrees (elbow); wrist flexion 80-90, extension 70-90, radial deviation 15, ulnar deviation 30-45; finger flexion MCP 85-90, PIP 100-115, DIP 80-90; finger extension MCP 30-45, PIP 0, DIP 20; finger abduction 20-30, adduction 0; thumb flexion CMC 45-50, MCP 50-55, IP 85-90; thumb extension MCP 0, IP 0-5; thumb abduction 60-70, adduction 30; opposition = thumb reaches the little finger.
positive: Not a pass/fail test: note pain, limitation versus the standard values and compensatory strategies.

accuracy.source: n/a (basic assessment; page lists no references)

notes: Basic assessment page. Companion pages: passive ROM and resisted isometric testing of the wrist/hand.

title: Wrist/Hand Passive Range of Motion
purpose: Basic passive range of motion (PROM) assessment of the wrist and hand, done when AROM is limited, to obtain the end-feel and find what limits motion.
procedure: Move each joint passively to the end of range and judge the end-feel. Normal end-feels listed on the page: wrist extension and flexion = tissue stretch; radial and ulnar deviation = hard; finger flexion and extension (all joints) = tissue stretch; thumb flexion and extension (all joints) = tissue stretch; thumb abduction (CMC) = tissue stretch; thumb adduction (CMC) = tissue approximation.
positive: Not a pass/fail test: an abnormal end-feel or limitation compared with the normal end-feel and the other side.

accuracy.source: n/a (basic assessment). Reference listed: Pourahmadi et al. 2017, reliability of an iPhone goniometer app for active wrist ROM

notes: Basic assessment page. The page mentions a table of normal/abnormal end-feels that is not reproduced in the API text. Companion page: active ROM of the wrist/hand.

title: Wrist/Hand Resisted Isometric Testing
purpose: Basic resisted isometric strength testing of the wrist, hand, fingers and thumb, performed after AROM and PROM.
structure: Wrist flexors/extensors (forearm muscles attaching to the humeral epicondyles), radial/ulnar deviators, finger flexors/extensors/abductors/adductors, thumb abductors/adductors/extensors/flexors; pronation and supination are covered on the elbow page.
procedure: Patient sits with the forearm on the bench. Wrist extension: fixate the distal forearm, resist on the dorsum of the hand. Wrist flexion: resist on the palm. Radial/ulnar deviation (patient may make a fist): fixate the distal forearm and resist movement towards the thumb / towards the little finger. Finger flexion: a firm handshake (or resist individual joints). Finger extension: hand flat on the bench, your hand on the fingers, patient lifts your hand. Finger abduction/adduction: intertwine your fingers with the patient's and resist spreading / squeezing. Thumb: fixate the hand including the scaphoid, make a fist around the thumb; abduction = movement perpendicular to the palm, adduction = towards the palm, extension = in the plane of the palm towards the radius, flexion = in the plane of the palm towards the ulna.
positive: Not a pass/fail test: weakness or pain compared with the other side.

accuracy.source: n/a (basic assessment; page lists no references)

notes: Basic assessment page. ⚠ Source typos: 'radial and medial deviation' (ulnar), and 'Finger abduction' is listed twice where the first item (squeeze the fingers) is adduction.

title: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Cluster
purpose: Clinical prediction rule (Wainner et al. 2005) to diagnose carpal tunnel syndrome and separate it from cervical radiculopathy.
structure: Median nerve in the carpal tunnel.
procedure: Score five items: (1) Flick sign (shaking the hand relieves symptoms); (2) wrist-ratio index > 0.67 (anteroposterior / mediolateral wrist width in cm, measured with a caliper); (3) Brigham and Women's Hospital Hand Symptom Severity Scale (SSS) score > 1.9 (11 items, 6 domains); (4) diminished sensation on the thumb pad compared with the base of the thenar eminence; (5) age over 45 years.
positive: Count of positive items: fewer than 2 of 5 argues against CTS; 4 of 5 or 5 of 5 confirm.

accuracy.source: Wainner et al. 2005 (Arch Phys Med Rehabil)

notes: Source: high clinical value to confirm CTS. CTS prevalence quoted as 3% in women, 2% in men. Common tests (ULTT A+B, Phalen, Tinel, abductor pollicis brevis strength) did not make it into the cluster because their validity was too low.

title: Flick Sign
purpose: History finding for carpal tunnel syndrome: does the patient shake (flick) the hand to ease pain and paraesthesia?
procedure: Ask whether the patient flicks the affected hand to relieve symptoms, like shaking down a thermometer; more a history item than a special test.
positive: Shaking the hand and wrist reduces the symptoms.

accuracy.source: D'Arcy & McGee 2000 systematic review (JAMA) citing Pryse-Phillips 1984; Hansen et al. 2004 (Am J Phys Med Rehabil)

notes: The original figures could not be reproduced; source rates the sign as weak on its own but it is one item of the Wainner 2005 CTS cluster. Krendel 1986 also listed.

title: Phalen’s Test
purpose: Provocation test for carpal tunnel syndrome.
structure: Median nerve in the carpal tunnel.
procedure: Patient standing or sitting, maximally flexes both wrists by pressing the dorsal sides of the hands together and holds for one minute.
positive: Reproduction of paraesthesia in the median nerve distribution (thumb, index, middle finger and/or radial half of the ring finger).

accuracy.source: Valdes & LaStayo 2013 literature review (J Hand Ther)

notes: Source: rather weak clinical value; excluded from the Wainner CTS cluster for low predictive ability; stand-alone tests add little to a thorough history. The page writes 'medial half of the ring finger' (the median nerve supplies the radial half).

title: Tinel Sign
purpose: Nerve percussion sign at the wrist for carpal tunnel syndrome.
procedure: Patient sitting with forearm and hand on the bench; tap the median nerve at the wrist with two fingers. Some authors tap along the whole median nerve from the index finger to the medial forearm.
positive: Tingling in the thumb, index, middle finger and/or radial half of the ring finger.

accuracy.source: Valdes & LaStayo 2013 (J Hand Ther); Montgomery et al. 2020 (J Hand Surg Am)

notes: Source: weak clinical value; use a validated cluster instead. The page writes 'medial half of the ring finger'.

title: Carpal Compression Test
purpose: Provocation test for carpal tunnel syndrome by direct pressure on the carpal tunnel.
structure: Median nerve in the carpal tunnel.
procedure: Forearm supinated; compress the carpal tunnel between your thenar and hypothenar eminences for 30 seconds.
positive: Paraesthesia, numbness or dull pain in the median nerve territory.

accuracy.source: Almasi-Doghaee et al. 2016 (Iran J Neurol); Fowler 2015 and Amirfeyz 2011 also listed

notes: Source: weak clinical value despite being more accurate than Tinel and Phalen; definitive diagnosis needs nerve conduction / EMG.

title: Hand Elevation Test
purpose: Provocation test for carpal tunnel syndrome.
structure: Median nerve in the carpal tunnel.
procedure: Patient standing or sitting raises both hands above the head and holds them there until paraesthesia, numbness or dull pain appears in the median nerve territory (lateral palm and palmar surface of the lateral three and a half fingers).

accuracy.source: Ma & Kim 2012 (J Korean Neurosurg Soc), single study

notes: Ma et al. argue it is the most accurate physical test for CTS, but the values have not been reproduced; source gives moderate clinical value for now.

title: TFCC Compression Test
purpose: Provocation test for a tear of the triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC).
structure: TFCC: articular disc, meniscus homologue, dorsal and palmar radioulnar ligaments, ulnolunate and ulnotriquetral ligaments, extensor carpi ulnaris tendon sheath.
procedure: Fixate the radius and ulna close to the joint line with one hand. Grasp the hand at the metacarpals from the radial side and bring the wrist into ulnar deviation under axial compression (Prosser et al. 2011).
positive: Reproduction of the patient's pain with a click or crepitus.

accuracy.source: none; page states no statistical values are described

notes: Source: questionable clinical value. Companion TFCC tests: fovea sign, ulnar grinding test.

title: Fovea Sign
purpose: Palpation sign for TFCC lesions (ulnar fovea).
structure: Ulnar fovea: soft spot between the ulnar styloid, flexor carpi ulnaris tendon, volar ulnar head and pisiform.
procedure: Palpate the soft spot between the ulnar styloid, the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon, the volar surface of the ulnar head and the pisiform.
positive: Reproducible pain at this spot compared with the contralateral side.

accuracy.source: Schmauss et al. 2016 (Arch Orthop Trauma Surg), 908 patients

notes: Source: rather weak; MRI performed no better in the same study (high sensitivity, poor specificity). Results varied slightly by Palmer classification (traumatic vs degenerative). The page has a figure caption (Rekant 2019) whose image is not in the API text.

title: Ulnar Grinding Test
structure: TFCC (centre of forearm rotation; load transmission to the wrist).
procedure: Forearm fixed, wrist held in dorsiflexion (extension). Apply an axial load while rotating the wrist and deviating it to the ulnar side.

accuracy.source: Schmauss et al. 2016 (Arch Orthop Trauma Surg)

notes: Source: rather weak diagnostic value because of poor specificity; MRI did not perform better. The page's figure caption (Rekant 2019, Palmer classification) has no image in the API text.

title: DRUJ Test
purpose: Assess a ligament tear / instability of the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ).
structure: Distal radioulnar joint and its ligaments.
procedure: Forearm in neutral rotation; stabilise the distal radius and hand as one unit with a firm grip. With the other hand grasp the distal ulna and force it dorsally and palmarly relative to the radius. Repeat in relative supination and pronation.
positive: Marked laxity compared with the uninjured wrist and reproduction of the patient's painful symptoms.

accuracy.source: Prosser et al. 2011 (J Physiother), vs arthroscopy

notes: Source: at most mildly useful to exclude an injury, overall weak. ⚠ The page's accuracy sentence says Prosser 'evaluated the Lunotriquetral Ballottement Test' while giving the DRUJ figures, a copy error from the LT page.

title: Watson Test
purpose: Scaphoid shift test for scapholunate (SL) ligament rupture / instability.
structure: Scapholunate ligament; untreated tears can lead to DISI (dorsal intercalated segmental instability).
procedure: Patient sitting, elbow supported, facing you. Fixate the radius with one hand and press your thumb dorsally on the palmar prominence of the scaphoid; the other hand grasps the metacarpals from the ulnar side. Start in ulnar deviation and slight extension (scaphoid long axis in line with the radius), then move into radial deviation and slight flexion while keeping thumb pressure. Release the thumb.
positive: A dorsal shift/subluxation of the scaphoid and a 'thunk' when the thumb is released, or reproduction of the familiar dorsal wrist pain. In a healthy wrist radial deviation is simply limited or the scaphoid pushes the thumb away palmarly.

accuracy.source: Valdes & LaStayo 2013 literature review (J Hand Ther)

notes: Source: moderate value to rule out an SL tear, low value to confirm it. SL injury can accompany distal radius or carpal fractures.

title: Lunotriquetral Ballotement Test
purpose: Shuck test for lunotriquetral (LT) ligament injury.
procedure: Patient sitting with forearm and hand on the table. Dorsopalmar shear: grasp the lunate with the fingers of one hand and the adjacent triquetrum with the other; fixate the lunate and glide the triquetrum dorsally and palmarly.
positive: Noticeable laxity compared with the unaffected hand and reproduction of the painful symptoms.

accuracy.source: Prosser et al. 2011 (J Physiother), vs arthroscopy

notes: Source: weak clinical value. Missed wrist ligament injuries can lead to persistent pain, instability, reduced grip and early osteoarthritis.

title: Midcarpal Test
purpose: Test for palmar midcarpal instability (arcuate / deltoid / V-ligament damage).
structure: Arcuate (deltoid, V) ligament joining the proximal and distal carpal rows; kinematic dysfunction of the proximal row.
procedure: Patient sits with the arm on the table, wrist in radial deviation. Grasp the hand so your thumb lies over the dorsal distal capitate, apply a palmarly directed force so the carpal bones translate palmarly, then move the wrist into ulnar deviation while maintaining the pressure.
positive: A painful clunk as the wrist moves from radial to ulnar deviation.

accuracy.source: Prosser et al. 2011 (J Physiother), vs arthroscopy; only LR+ reported

notes: Source: weak clinical value; a positive result is at most mildly useful.
